## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.38704.024](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.38704.024)

In the interests of transparency, eLife includes the editorial decision letter and accompanying author responses. A lightly edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the most substantive concerns; minor comments are not usually included.

Thank you for submitting your article "Insulin regulates POMC neuronal plasticity to control glucose metabolism" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Mark McCarthy as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal his identity: Dong Kong (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

This interesting manuscript presents a large amount of information regarding the role of a specific protein tyrosine phosphatase, TCPTP, in the control of insulin responsiveness in POMC neurons in relation to control of systemic insulin sensitivity and hepatic glucose metabolism. The data strongly suggest both a key role for TCPTP in the responsiveness of POMC cells to insulin and that enhanced insulin signaling depolarizes and increases the firing of in these neurons, while the opposite effect is observed in POMC neurons with high levels of TCPTP. The data also offer a welcome new perspective on the role of POMC neurons in the control of HGP and a potential resolution to controversy surrounding this issue stemming from earlier work, and the impact of changes in nutritional state on POMC cell insulin responsiveness is also novel and of interest.

The reviewers of this paper found the results to be of great interest and suitable for publication in eLife after some revisions. It was not possible to assemble the comments into a few key points for consideration (eLife normal procedure) because the three reviewers had non-overlapping concerns. Thus, all of the comments are included below. The reviewers had a number of concerns that can, in general, be addressed without further experiments. However, explanations of the many points raised are necessary and caveats to the data interpretation should be included. Additional experiments that address concerns are, of course, welcome.

One issue raised by reviewers is that the use of Pomc-Cre mice is problematic because Cre recombinase is activated in neurons that go to develop into AgRP (and other) neurons. Thus, some of the data are probably derived from a mixed population of arcuate neurons.

The other issue is that the mitochondria data are correlative and do not provide compelling evidence linking mitochondrial dynamics and glucose regulation. Some reviewers, including the editor, suggest either providing a causal link between mitochondrial dynamics and glucose regulation, or removing the mitochondrial experiments from this story.

The authors should define TCPTP on first usage and note the mouse gene names do not include hyphens, e.g. Il6, not Il-6.

Reviewer #1:

In this study, Dodd et al. investigate the role of TCPTP in POMC neurons upon insulin signaling and glucose metabolism control. The authors report a correlation between TCPTP expression in POMC neurons and the level of neuron responsiveness to insulin. High expression of TCPTP in obesity or fasting hampers insulin-induced signaling, POMC neuron activation and repression of HGP. In contrast, genetic inactivation of TCPTP in POMC neurons causes enhanced insulin-stimulated signaling, activation of POMC neurons and inhibition of HGP. The authors also report changes in mitochondrial dynamics and mitochondria-ER contacts in POMC neurons upon TCPTP deletion. The authors propose that physiological (fed/fast) and pathophysiological (HFD) changes in TCPTP expression in POMC neurons may influence neuronal activity and HGP via insulin signaling-mediated modulation of mitochondrial fusion and contacts with the ER.

The study uses a nice combination of mouse genetics, electrophysiology, pharmacology as well as physiological and molecular biology techniques. Generally speaking, the conclusions are supported by the data although some statements in specific parts of the manuscript should be softened. Overall, the study fulfils the highest standards in the field and seems appropriate for publication in eLife.

I do not have major concerns that require additional experiments but I would suggest further analysis of the electrophysiology results. In particular, the authors compare the number (population size) of POMC neurons that are activated, inhibited or unresponsive to insulin amongst a number of experimental settings. Table 1 provides statistical comparisons for some of these studies, but not all (only for KO's and double Ko's). However, the authors claim that pharmacological TCPTP inhibition "significantly altered POMC responses to insulin" but statistical evidence is not provided. The same for the HFD study. The authors should provide a complete table of comparisons amongst the diverse experimental settings.

Reviewer #2:

Insulin's effect on POMC neurons, their neuronal heterogeneity, and the related blood glucose regulation have been interesting topics in the field of brain-controlled metabolism for quite a while. However, the underlying mechanisms are still unclear. Whether POMC neurons regulate glucose homeostasis is also under debate. In the current study, Dodd et al. focused on these questions, performed a series of studies, and made multiple important and exciting findings. First, they documented heterogenous responses of POMC neurons to insulin and further demonstrated a dependence of such responses on the expression of TCPTP phosphatase in these neurons. Then, the author performed glucose clamp studies by combining with chemogenetic tools and assessed the peripheral mechanisms. They found that TCPTP in POMC neurons regulated blood glucose by mainly inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Finally, they also used multiple mouse models and discovered that feeding/fasting and HFD-feeding induced TCPTP expression in POMC neurons regulated insulin receptor signaling and mitochondrial dynamics to manipulate responses to insulin and peripheral glucose homeostasis.

Overall, this manuscript is very well prepared, the studies were properly designed, performed, and analyzed, and the conclusions were well reached. The current study has thus established an elegant system to understand the central control of glucose metabolism. I believe the manuscript will be of great interest to the readers of eLife and I have the following comments for the authors to address.

1) The authors performed a large number of current-clamp recordings on POMC neurons to assess their responses to insulin. However, the results of membrane potential seem problematic in the current study. For example, in the first paragraph of the subsection “TCPTP defines POMC neurons that are activated or inhibited by insulin”, POMC neurons after insulin stimulation exhibited an averaged membrane potential of -40.1+/-2.5 mV; in the next paragraph of the aforementioned subsection, excited neurons had a membrane potential as depolarized as -37.9+/-1.7 mV. How could POMC neurons be so depolarized?

2) As shown previously by Padilla, Carmody and Zeltser, et al. (Nat Med 2010, and in a more convincing way recently by Xu et al., 2018, POMC-Cre exhibited ectopic Cre activity during development, particularly in AgRP neuron. Breeding Pomc-Cre with floxed mice could yield a manipulation of 25% AgRP neurons as well (Xu et al.). In Figure 1G-H, since the authors used Z/EG reporter instead of Pomc-eGFP transgenic mice to indicate POMC neurons, AgRP neurons were expected to be patched on as well. Since AgRP neurons are known to be inhibited by insulin, the ratio for the insulin-inhibited POMC neurons (12/33, 36.4%) may need to be adjusted.

3) Subsection “The activation or inhibition of POMC neurons regulates hepatic glucose metabolism”, the authors utilized inhibitory DREADDs to inhibit POMC neurons and included convincing expression data of hM4Di in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. However, a direct test of CNO's activity on POMC neurons with current-clamp recording shall also be included since hM4Di works through the activation of GIRK channels and not all neurons express them. In addition, CNO was recently reported to activate other endogenous receptors as well (Gomez et al., Science 2017). CNO's effects on non-DREADD-expressing animals shall also be included as a control.

4) In the third paragraph of the Discussion, the authors discussed about the potential mechanisms with regards to synaptic regulation. Deletion of TCPTP in POMC neurons clearly suggested a post-synaptic mechanism but the authors believed in an existence of pre-synaptic regulation. This is confusing. Do the authors think of the involvement of a retrograde mechanism or different action sites of TCPTP from POMC neurons?

Reviewer #3:

This interesting manuscript presents a large amount of information regarding the role of a specific protein tyrosine phosphatase, TCPTP, in the control of insulin responsiveness in POMC neurons in relation to control of systemic insulin sensitivity and hepatic glucose metabolism. The data strongly suggest both a key role for TCPTP in the responsiveness of POMC cells to insulin and that enhanced insulin signaling depolarizes and increases the firing of in these neurons, while the opposite effect is observed in POMC neurons with high levels of TCPTP. The data also offer a welcome new perspective on the role of POMC neurons in the control of HGP and a potential resolution to controversy surrounding this issue stemming from earlier work, and the impact of changes in nutritional state on POMC cell insulin responsiveness is also novel and of interest. These considerable strengths are offset to some extent by the following concerns.

1) A key unanswered question is how increased insulin receptor signal transduction associated with reduced TCPTP is tied to a reversal of the effect of insulin on POMC neuron membrane potential and firing rate (from inhibitory to stimulatory). The authors state that this "phenotype switch" in the insulin response reflects direct (rather than an indirect) effects of insulin, but how increased IR-PI3K-Akt signal transduction in these cells might achieve this effect is unresolved. In an effort to shed light on this key question, the authors investigate whether changes in POMC cell mitochondrial dynamics underlie this phenotype switch. Although changes of insulin responsiveness appear to be coupled to morphological and genomic alterations affecting mitochondria, the data fail to establish a connection between these mitochondrial responses and changes of membrane potential and firing rate. Consequently, the data on mitochondrial dynamics seem somewhat disconnected from the rest of the paper, and might be more appropriate for a separate publication.

2) The authors finding of a robust effect of POMC-specific TCPTP deletion to enhance insulin suppression of HGP begs the question as to what other responses to insulin might also be affected. Given that ICV insulin has previously been reported to reduce food intake, body weight and body adiposity, and that brain-specific IR deletion promotes positive energy balance and weight gain, one wonders whether the effect of ICV insulin on food intake, body weight and body adiposity are also increased. Given the marked improvement of whole-body insulin sensitivity attributed to POMC-specific TCPTP deletion, one also wonders why the basal glucose and insulin levels were not reduced in these animals.

3) A related question is whether reduced body adiposity results from POMC-specific TCPTP deletion, and if so, did this contribute to enhanced insulin-induced suppression of HGP reported by the authors? Conversely, if POMC-specific TCPTP deletion has no effect on energy balance or body adiposity, this seems surprising given the expected increase of POMC neuron firing.

4) The question of how pronounced changes of POMC expression of TCPTP are associated with feeding, fasting and DIO was not addressed. Doing so would considerably strengthen the manuscript and seems of much greater relevance than the large amount of mitochondrial data that were included.

5) During embryogenesis, the POMC promoter is expressed in multiple arcuate nucleus neuronal subtypes including AgRP neurons. Since POMC-Cre was used to delete TCPTP, one expects the gene to be deleted across multiple arcuate nucleus neuronal cell types. Some effort to address this concern is warranted.

6) The authors state that diet-induced obesity reduces POMC neuron insulin responsiveness via a mechanism involving induction of TCPTP. Is this effect of DIO causally linked to associated responses such as inflammation, reactive gliosis, ER stress, etc.? Discussion of this question seems warranted.

7) The authors report (Discussion, last paragraph) that TCPTP deletion has no detectable effect on glucose homeostasis in DIO mice, which they attribute to the fact that other mechanisms can account for impaired POMC insulin responsiveness in this setting. But they stop short of investigating whether TCPTP deletion enhances insulin responsiveness to POMC neurons in this setting. This question should be addressed since, if POMC neuron insulin responsiveness is in fact restored and yet there is no whole-body phenotype, the physiological relevance of POMC neuron insulin responsiveness would be called into question.

8) What precedent exists for a change in hormone responsiveness reversing its effect on the firing of a distinct neuronal subset? If such a response has been reported previously, was it referred to as "neural plasticity"? Certainly, this is not the type of response that comes to mind in association with that term. In this context, the term "neural plasticity" seems potentially misleading and for this reason, it is recommended that it be removed from the manuscript title.

9) The effect of IP insulin to induce c-Fos in the PVH (Figure 1M) could have resulted from hypoglycemia, which was presumably well established by 90 min following the dose of insulin that was given. The effect of neuroglucopenia to activate PVH neurons is well established (e.g., Briski, Neuroreport, 1998; Briski, Brain Res Bulletin, 2000; Evans, AJP, 2001), and it is conceivable that changes of POMC cell insulin responsiveness affected the degree of insulin-induced hypoglycemia.

10) When insulin is given ICV and HGP or other highly insulin-responsive endpoints are measured, it's important to verify that none of the centrally-administered insulin leaked into the periphery to have direct effects on the liver.

11) Relevant to this point is the use of a study design in which ICV insulin (0.1 mU) or vehicle was given as 5 separate injections over 5 hours. It is difficult to imagine that 5 ICV injections over 5 hours would be well-tolerated, which in turn raises the possibility that the authors were inadvertently measuring the impact of insulin on a stress response, which might explain the basal hyperglycemia reported in some studies. Beyond this, insulin in CSF has a relatively long half-life, so it's not clear why a repeated injection protocol over 5 hours was required. Were the animals anesthetized during this period? I could not find the information in the Materials and methods section.

12) The basal glucose level (time=0 min) of both groups in the pyruvate tolerance test shown in Figure 2C is ~12 mM, which is in the diabetic range. By comparison, basal glucose levels of 7 mM are reported for the same test in Figure 2J, and are uniformly <10 mM in all other such studies (Figures 4, 5 and 6). This discrepancy is all the more notable in light of the remarkably small variances (SEMs) around the glucose data, which is inconsistent with known biological variability inherent in the response.

13) The Discussion is longer than it need be, and tends to reiterate points made in the Results section. It could be cut substantially.

claims.source: Insulin binds to its tyrosine kinase receptor and signals via the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase PKB/AKT pathway to hyperpolarise and inhibit AgRP/NPY neurons and repress Agrp expression (Könner et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 2000; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Könner et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 2000; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Vogt and Brüning, 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Leptin hyperpolarizes and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons and represses Npy/Agrp expression.
claims.source: Leptin also hyperpolarizes and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons and represses Npy/Agrp expression acting via several pathways, including the Janus-activated kinase (JAK)−2/signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT)−3 pathway and the PI3K/AKT pathway (Cowley et al., 2001; Elias et al., 1999; van den Top et al., 2004; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Cowley et al., 2001; Elias et al., 1999; van den Top et al., 2004; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).

claims.claim: IR signaling in AgRP neurons is important for the control of peripheral glucose metabolism.
claims.source: IR signaling in AgRP neurons is important for the control of peripheral glucose metabolism (Dodd et al., 2018; Könner et al., 2007) acting through vagal efferents to the liver and α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors to repress hepatic glucose production (HGP) (Kimura et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations (Dodd et al., 2018; Könner et al., 2007; Kimura et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Central insulin signaling suppresses HGP by activating Kupffer cells to release interleukin-6 (IL-6).
claims.source: Central insulin signaling suppresses HGP by activating Kupffer cells to release interleukin- 6 (IL-6) (Obici et al., 2002a; Obici et al., 2002b; Pocai et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations (Obici et al., 2002a; Obici et al., 2002b; Pocai et al., 2005).

claims.claim: IL-6 acts on hepatocytes via STAT-3 to repress the expression of gluconeogenic enzymes such as glucose-6-phosphatase (encoded by G6pc).
claims.source: IL-6 in turn acts on hepatocytes via STAT-3 to repress the expression of gluconeogenic enzymes such as glucose-6-phosphatase (encoded by G6pc) (Inoue et al., 2006; Inoue et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations (Inoue et al., 2006; Inoue et al., 2004).

claims.claim: IR deletion in AgRP neurons in mice results in defective inhibition of HGP accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased G6pc hepatic gene expression.
claims.source: IR deletion in AgRP neurons in mice results in defective inhibition of HGP accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased G6pc hepatic gene expression (Könner et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Könner et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Leptin depolarises and activates POMC neurons and promotes Pomc expression and α-MSH secretion to repress feeding, increase energy expenditure and repress HGP.
claims.source: Leptin depolarises and activates POMC neurons and promotes Pomc expression and α-MSH secretion to repress feeding, increase energy expenditure and repress HGP (Berglund et al., 2012; Caron et al., 2018; Varela and Horvath, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations (Berglund et al., 2012; Caron et al., 2018; Varela and Horvath, 2012).

claims.claim: Insulin has been traditionally viewed as an inhibitor of POMC neuronal excitation, hyperpolarising POMC neurons through the engagement of ATP-sensitive K+ channels.
claims.source: By contrast insulin has been traditionally viewed as an inhibitor of POMC neuronal excitation, hyperpolarising POMC neurons through the engagement of ATP-sensitive K+ channels (Hill et al., 2008; Könner et al., 2007; Plum et al., 2006; Spanswick et al., 2000; Williams et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Hill et al., 2008; Könner et al., 2007; Plum et al., 2006; Spanswick et al., 2000; Williams et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Insulin can depolarise and activate POMC neurons via the activation of transient receptor potential (TRPC)−5 channels.
claims.source: More recent studies have shown that insulin can depolarise and activate POMC neurons via the activation of transient receptor potential (TRPC)−5 channels (Qiu et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2014), whereas several studies have shown that insulin can promote Pomc expression and the melanocortin response (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations (Qiu et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Insulin can promote Pomc expression and the melanocortin response.
claims.source: More recent studies have shown that insulin can depolarise and activate POMC neurons via the activation of transient receptor potential (TRPC)−5 channels (Qiu et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2014), whereas several studies have shown that insulin can promote Pomc expression and the melanocortin response (Varela and Horvath, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varela and Horvath, 2012.

claims.claim: Single-cell transcriptomics has led to the identification of different subsets of POMC- and AgRP-expressing neurons that exhibit distinct transcriptional responses to changing energy status.
claims.source: The advent of single-cell transcriptomics has yielded unprecedented insight into the heterogeneity of hypothalamic cell types and has led to the identification of different subsets of POMC- and AgRP-expressing neurons that exhibit distinct transcriptional responses to changing energy status (Campbell et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Henry et al., 2015; Lam et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Campbell et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Henry et al., 2015; Lam et al., 2017).

claims.claim: IR deletion in POMC neurons does not influence glucose metabolism.
claims.source: Irrespective, whereas insulin signaling in AgRP neurons overtly affects glucose metabolism through the control of HGP and brown adipose tissue glucose uptake (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017), gene deletion and pharmacogenetic experiments have suggested that insulin signaling in POMC neurons may not be so important; neither IR deletion in POMC neurons (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017) nor the acute activation of POMC neurons using DREADDs (Steculorum et al., 2016) influences glucose metabolism.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The acute activation of POMC neurons using DREADDs does not influence glucose metabolism.
claims.source: Irrespective, whereas insulin signaling in AgRP neurons overtly affects glucose metabolism through the control of HGP and brown adipose tissue glucose uptake (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017), gene deletion and pharmacogenetic experiments have suggested that insulin signaling in POMC neurons may not be so important; neither IR deletion in POMC neurons (Könner et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2017) nor the acute activation of POMC neurons using DREADDs (Steculorum et al., 2016) influences glucose metabolism.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Steculorum et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The combined deletion of the IR plus leptin receptor in POMC neurons profoundly affects glucose homeostasis and results in systemic insulin resistance and increased HGP.
claims.source: Nonetheless, the combined deletion of the IR plus leptin receptor in POMC neurons profoundly affects glucose homeostasis and results in systemic insulin resistance and increased HGP (Hill et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hill et al., 2010.

claims.claim: TCPTP is an IR phosphatase whose abundance in the ARC is increased by fasting and repressed by feeding.
claims.source: We report that insulin can elicit discordant effects on the electrophysiological activity of POMC neurons and that this is regulated by T-cell protein tyrosine phosphatase (TCPTP) (Tiganis, 2013), an IR phosphatase whose abundance in the ARC is increased by fasting and repressed by feeding (Dodd et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations (Tiganis, 2013; Dodd et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The majority of POMC neurons from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP reporter mice were either inhibited by insulin (27/53, 50.9%) or were unaffected by insulin (20/53, 37.7%).
claims.source: The majority of POMC neurons were either inhibited by insulin (27/53, 50.9%) with a significant membrane hyperpolarisation (baseline −42.5 ± 1.2 mV; insulin −45.9 ± 1.8 mV) and decreased firing rate (baseline 1.09 ± 0.20 Hz; insulin 0.2 ± 0.06 Hz) or were unaffected by insulin (20/53, 37.7%) with minimal changes in membrane potential (baseline −46.8 ± 1.7 mV; insulin −45.7 ± 1.8 mV) and non-significant changes in firing rate (baseline 1.32 ± 0.51 Hz; insulin 1.08 ± 0.41 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claims.claim: A smaller subset of POMC neurons (6/53, 11.3%) from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP reporter mice were activated by insulin.
claims.source: A smaller subset of POMC neurons (6/53, 11.3%) were activated by insulin exhibiting significant membrane depolarisation (baseline −45.9 ± 2.4 mV; insulin −40.1 ± 2.5 mV) and increased firing rates (baseline 0.99 ± 0.37 Hz; insulin 1.69 ± 0.60 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claims.claim: Insulin-inhibited POMC neurons exhibited significant membrane hyperpolarisation (baseline −42.5 ± 1.2 mV; insulin −45.9 ± 1.8 mV) and decreased firing rate (baseline 1.09 ± 0.20 Hz; insulin 0.2 ± 0.06 Hz).
claims.source: The majority of POMC neurons were either inhibited by insulin (27/53, 50.9%) with a significant membrane hyperpolarisation (baseline −42.5 ± 1.2 mV; insulin −45.9 ± 1.8 mV) and decreased firing rate (baseline 1.09 ± 0.20 Hz; insulin 0.2 ± 0.06 Hz) or were unaffected by insulin (20/53, 37.7%) with minimal changes in membrane potential (baseline −46.8 ± 1.7 mV; insulin −45.7 ± 1.8 mV) and non-significant changes in firing rate (baseline 1.32 ± 0.51 Hz; insulin 1.08 ± 0.41 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claims.claim: Insulin-activated POMC neurons exhibited significant membrane depolarisation (baseline −45.9 ± 2.4 mV; insulin −40.1 ± 2.5 mV) and increased firing rates (baseline 0.99 ± 0.37 Hz; insulin 1.69 ± 0.60 Hz).
claims.source: A smaller subset of POMC neurons (6/53, 11.3%) were activated by insulin exhibiting significant membrane depolarisation (baseline −45.9 ± 2.4 mV; insulin −40.1 ± 2.5 mV) and increased firing rates (baseline 0.99 ± 0.37 Hz; insulin 1.69 ± 0.60 Hz, Figure 1a–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1a-c.

claims.claim: Excited POMC neurons were located more medially and comparatively closer to the third ventricle.
claims.source: Although the unresponsive and inhibited POMC neurons did not exhibit any distinct anatomical distribution, the excited POMC neurons were located more medially and comparatively closer to the third ventricle. (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the camera lucida image in Figure 1d showing the topographical localization of insulin-responsive POMC neuronal subtypes.

claims.claim: The majority of inhibited (25/27) and around half of all unresponsive (11/20) POMC neurons in patch-clamped coronal slices from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP mice expressed TCPTP.
claims.source: We found that the majority of inhibited (25/27) and around half of all unresponsive (11/20) POMC neurons in the patch-clamped coronal slices from ad libitum fed Pomc-eGFP mice expressed TCPTP (Figure 1e–f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1e-f.

claims.claim: Most (5/6) of POMC neurons that were excited by insulin did not express TCPTP.
claims.source: On the other hand, most (5/6) of POMC neurons that were excited by insulin did not express TCPTP (Figure 1f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1f.

claims.claim: TCPTP-deficiency significantly increased the number of POMC neurons that were excited (12/33, 36.4%) in response to insulin.
claims.source: Strikingly TCPTP-deficiency significantly increased the number of cells that were excited (12/33, 36.4%) in response to insulin and decreased the number of inhibited (12/33, 36.4%) POMC neurons; TCPTP-deficiency tended to decrease the number of unresponsive (9/33, 27.3%) POMC neurons but this was not significant (Figure 1g–h; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in POMC-TC mice shown in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: TCPTP-deficiency decreased the number of inhibited (12/33, 36.4%) POMC neurons.
claims.source: Strikingly TCPTP-deficiency significantly increased the number of cells that were excited (12/33, 36.4%) in response to insulin and decreased the number of inhibited (12/33, 36.4%) POMC neurons; TCPTP-deficiency tended to decrease the number of unresponsive (9/33, 27.3%) POMC neurons but this was not significant (Figure 1g–h; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in POMC-TC mice shown in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons activated by insulin increased to 33% (19/58 cells).
claims.source: Strikingly, TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons activated by insulin increased to 33% (19/58 cells) (Figure 1i; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Pomc-eGFP mice treated with TCPTP inhibitor shown in Figure 1i.

claims.claim: In high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons inhibited by insulin increased from 51% (27/53 cells) to 65% (22/34 cells).
claims.source: Consistent with this, we found that in high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons inhibited by insulin ex vivo increased from 51% (27/53 cells) to 65% (22/34 cells; p=0.045; Supplementary file 2), whereas the proportion of cells being activated fell from 11% (6/53 cells) to 3% (1/34 cells; p=0.027, Figure 1k; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice shown in Figure 1k.

claims.claim: In high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of POMC neurons being activated by insulin fell from 11% (6/53 cells) to 3% (1/34 cells).
claims.source: Consistent with this, we found that in high-fat-fed obese mice the proportion of GFP-positive POMC neurons inhibited by insulin ex vivo increased from 51% (27/53 cells) to 65% (22/34 cells; p=0.045; Supplementary file 2), whereas the proportion of cells being activated fell from 11% (6/53 cells) to 3% (1/34 cells; p=0.027, Figure 1k; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice shown in Figure 1k.

claims.claim: TCPTP inhibition in high-fat-fed mice significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that only 20% (7/35 cells) of GFP-positive POMC neurons were inhibited by insulin.
claims.source: Strikingly, TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that only 20% (7/35 cells) of GFP-positive POMC neurons were inhibited by insulin, whereas the proportion of cells being activated increased from 3% (1/34 cells) to 37% (13/35; p<0.001, Figure 1k–l; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice treated with TCPTP inhibitor shown in Figure 1k-l.

claims.claim: TCPTP inhibition in high-fat-fed mice increased the proportion of POMC neurons being activated by insulin from 3% (1/34 cells) to 37% (13/35).
claims.source: Strikingly, TCPTP inhibition significantly altered POMC responses to insulin such that only 20% (7/35 cells) of GFP-positive POMC neurons were inhibited by insulin, whereas the proportion of cells being activated increased from 3% (1/34 cells) to 37% (13/35; p<0.001, Figure 1k–l; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in high-fat fed mice treated with TCPTP inhibitor shown in Figure 1k-l.

claims.claim: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC-TC mice increased c-Fos staining in the PVH of fasted mice and this was exacerbated by insulin.
claims.source: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC-TC mice increased c-Fos staining (a surrogate marker of neuronal activation) in the PVH of fasted mice and this was exacerbated by insulin (Figure 1m); although systemic insulin administration resulted in hypoglycemia, this was similar in Ptpn2fl/fl and POMC-TC mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1m.

claims.claim: The acute inhibition of POMC neurons had no effect on HGP.
claims.source: We found that the acute inhibition of POMC neurons had no effect, whereas the inhibition of POMC neurons over 6 hr increased blood glucose levels in response to pyruvate, consistent with the promotion of HGP (Figure 2c); CNO had no effect on the electrophysiological response of non-DREADD expressing POMC neurons (data not shown) and did not alter glucose metabolism (as assessed by measuring glucose excursions in response to pyruvate, glucose or insulin) in C57BL/6 control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: The inhibition of POMC neurons over 6 hr increased blood glucose levels in response to pyruvate, consistent with the promotion of HGP.
claims.source: We found that the acute inhibition of POMC neurons had no effect, whereas the inhibition of POMC neurons over 6 hr increased blood glucose levels in response to pyruvate, consistent with the promotion of HGP (Figure 2c); CNO had no effect on the electrophysiological response of non-DREADD expressing POMC neurons (data not shown) and did not alter glucose metabolism (as assessed by measuring glucose excursions in response to pyruvate, glucose or insulin) in C57BL/6 control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: The chronic, but not acute inhibition of POMC neurons was accompanied by the significant repression of hepatic Il6 expression and diminished hepatic STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation.
claims.source: We found that the chronic, but not acute inhibition of POMC neurons was accompanied by the significant repression of hepatic Il6 expression and diminished hepatic STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation (Figure 2d–e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and qPCR data shown in Figure 2d-e.

claims.claim: Chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with increased expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc.
claims.source: This in turn was associated with increased expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: Chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with attenuated insulin-mediated repression of endogenous glucose production.
claims.source: We found that chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with attenuated insulin-mediated repression of endogenous glucose production and an overall decrease in insulin sensitivity as assessed by the reduced glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia during the clamp and the reduced glucose disappearance rate (Rd; Figure 2f–g; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2f-g.

claims.claim: Chronic POMC neuronal inhibition resulted in an overall decrease in insulin sensitivity as assessed by the reduced glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia during the clamp and the reduced glucose disappearance rate (Rd).
claims.source: We found that chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was associated with attenuated insulin-mediated repression of endogenous glucose production and an overall decrease in insulin sensitivity as assessed by the reduced glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia during the clamp and the reduced glucose disappearance rate (Rd; Figure 2f–g; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2f-g.

claims.claim: The attenuated repression of endogenous glucose production by chronic POMC neuronal inhibition was accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression.
claims.source: The attenuated repression of endogenous glucose production was accompanied by decreased Il6 and increased hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 2h), in keeping with the attenuated repression of HGP.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2h.

claims.claim: Chronic POMC neuronal activation resulted in the suppression of glucose excursion in response to pyruvate in keeping with the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis.
claims.source: Chronic but not acute POMC neuronal activation resulted in the suppression of glucose excursion in response to pyruvate (Figure 2j) in keeping with the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and was accompanied by elevated hepatic Il6 expression, increased STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation and the significant repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 2k–l).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2j.

claims.claim: Chronic POMC neuronal activation was accompanied by elevated hepatic Il6 expression, increased STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation and the significant repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression.
claims.source: Chronic but not acute POMC neuronal activation resulted in the suppression of glucose excursion in response to pyruvate (Figure 2j) in keeping with the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and was accompanied by elevated hepatic Il6 expression, increased STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation and the significant repression of Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 2k–l).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and qPCR data shown in Figure 2k-l.

claims.claim: TCPTP deletion in POMC neurons resulted in improved pyruvate tolerance at doses of insulin that elicited little to no effect in Ptpn2fl/fl control mice.
claims.source: At doses of insulin that elicited little to no effect in Ptpn2fl/fl control mice, we found that TCPTP deletion in POMC neurons resulted in improved pyruvate tolerance, as assessed by the suppression of pyruvate-induced increases in blood glucose levels (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: The improved pyruvate tolerance in POMC-TC mice was accompanied by increased ICV insulin-induced hypothalamic Pomc and hepatic Il6 gene expression as well as increased hepatic p-STAT-3.
claims.source: The improved pyruvate tolerance was accompanied by increased ICV insulin-induced hypothalamic Pomc and hepatic Il6 gene expression as well as increased hepatic p-STAT-3 (Figure 3c–e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3c-e.

claims.claim: The hepatic expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc expression was elevated in overnight fasted POMC-TC mice.
claims.source: The hepatic expression of the gluconeogenic genes Pck1 and G6pc expression was elevated in overnight fasted POMC-TC mice (Figure 3d), probably as a compensatory mechanism to prevent hypoglycemia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: The increased hepatic STAT3 signaling in ICV insulin-administered POMC-TC mice was associated with the increased repression of hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression.
claims.source: Nonetheless the increased hepatic STAT3 signaling in ICV insulin-administered POMC-TC mice was associated with the increased repression of hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons was accompanied by lower fasted (6 hr) blood glucose and plasma insulin levels.
claims.source: TCPTP-deficiency was accompanied by lower fasted (6 hr) blood glucose and plasma insulin levels, in keeping with overall improvements in glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity (Figure 4a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by blood glucose and plasma insulin measurements shown in Figure 4a-b.

claims.claim: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons resulted in greater reductions in blood glucose levels in response to insulin and improved glucose clearances in response to a bolus of glucose.
claims.source: This was reflected in greater reductions in blood glucose levels in response to insulin and improved glucose clearances in response to a bolus of glucose (Figure 4c–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by insulin and glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 4c-d.

claims.claim: Excursions in blood glucose in response to pyruvate were attenuated in POMC-TC mice in keeping with reduced endogenous glucose production.
claims.source: Moreover, excursions in blood glucose in response to pyruvate were attenuated in keeping with reduced endogenous glucose production (Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 4e.

claims.claim: The glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice, consistent with enhanced whole-body insulin sensitivity.
claims.source: We found that the glucose infusion rate (GIR) necessary to maintain euglycemia was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice, consistent with enhanced whole-body insulin sensitivity (Figure 4f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: The glucose disappearance rate (Rd) was unaltered by TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons under the conditions tested.
claims.source: Importantly we found that the glucose disappearance rate (Rd), which primarily measures muscle and adipose tissue glucose uptake, was unaltered by TCPTP-deficiency under the conditions tested, whereas the insulin-induced repression of endogenous glucose production, a measure of hepatic and renal glucose production, was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice (Figure 4f; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: The insulin-induced repression of endogenous glucose production was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice.
claims.source: Importantly we found that the glucose disappearance rate (Rd), which primarily measures muscle and adipose tissue glucose uptake, was unaltered by TCPTP-deficiency under the conditions tested, whereas the insulin-induced repression of endogenous glucose production, a measure of hepatic and renal glucose production, was significantly enhanced in POMC-TC mice (Figure 4f; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: The repressed endogenous glucose production in POMC-TC mice was accompanied by decreased expression of hepatic gluconeogenic genes (Pck1 and G6pc).
claims.source: The repressed endogenous glucose production was accompanied by decreased expression of hepatic gluconeogenic genes (Pck1 and G6pc, Figure 4g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4g.

claims.claim: Insulin-induced IR Y1162/Y1163 tyrosine phosphorylation and activation and downstream PI3K/AKT signaling in the liver were dramatically enhanced by POMC TCPTP deficiency.
claims.source: In keeping with the overall improvement in insulin sensitivity we found that insulin-induced IR Y1162/Y1163 tyrosine phosphorylation and activation and downstream PI3K/AKT signaling in the liver (as monitored by AKT Ser-473 phosphorylation) were dramatically enhanced by POMC TCPTP deficiency (Figure 4h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4h.

claims.claim: Insulin-induced PI3K/Akt signaling was not altered in skeletal muscle or white adipose tissue by POMC TCPTP deficiency.
claims.source: By contrast insulin-induced PI3K/Akt signaling was not altered in skeletal muscle or white adipose tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c-d.

claims.claim: In fed mice, ICV administered insulin repressed hepatic gluconeogenesis as assessed by the attenuated glucose excursions in response to pyruvate and the inhibition of gluconeogenic gene expression (Pck1 and G6pc).
claims.source: We found that in fed mice, ICV administered insulin repressed hepatic gluconeogenesis as assessed by the attenuated glucose excursions in response to pyruvate (Figure 5b) and the inhibition of gluconeogenic gene expression (Pck1 and G6pc; Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test and qPCR data shown in Figure 5b-c.

claims.claim: ICV insulin in fed mice was accompanied by the promotion of hepatic Il6 expression.
claims.source: This was accompanied by the promotion of hepatic Il6 expression (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: In food-restricted mice, ICV administered insulin had no effect on pyruvate-induced glucose excursions or the expression of Pck1, G6pc and Il6.
claims.source: By contrast, in food-restricted mice (Figure 5d), ICV administered insulin had no effect on pyruvate-induced glucose excursions (Figure 5e) or the expression of Pck1, G6pc and Il6 (Figure 5f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test and qPCR data shown in Figure 5e-f.

claims.claim: ICV insulin had no effect on glucose excursions in response to pyruvate in food-restricted Ptpn2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: As in food-restricted C57BL/6 mice, ICV insulin had no effect on glucose excursions in response to pyruvate in food-restricted Ptpn2fl/fl mice (Figure 5g), nor did it alter the expression of Pck1, G6pc or Il6 (Figure 5h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test and qPCR data shown in Figure 5g-h.

claims.claim: Glucose excursions in vehicle-treated POMC-TC mice were reduced relative to Ptpn2fl/fl mice and reduced further in response to ICV insulin administration.
claims.source: By contrast glucose excursions in vehicle-treated POMC-TC mice were reduced relative to Ptpn2fl/fl mice and reduced further in response to ICV insulin administration (Figure 5g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 5g.

claims.claim: ICV administered insulin dramatically reduced hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression below that in Ptpn2fl/fl controls in food-restricted POMC-TC mice and was accompanied by a greater than two-fold increase in Il6 expression.
claims.source: Nonetheless, ICV administered insulin dramatically reduced hepatic Pck1 and G6pc expression below that in Ptpn2fl/fl controls and was accompanied by a greater than two-fold increase in Il6 expression (Figure 5h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5h.

claims.claim: TCPTP deficiency enhanced insulin-induced ARC PI3K/AKT signaling in POMC neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous studies (Dodd et al., 2015) we found that TCPTP deficiency enhanced insulin-induced ARC PI3K/AKT signaling in POMC neurons, as assessed by monitoring for AKT Ser-473 phosphorylation (p-AKT) in mice on the Pomc-eGFP reporter background.
claims.evidence: This is supported by p-AKT immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a-b and citations (Dodd et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling otherwise associated with TCPTP-deficiency was significantly repressed, albeit not completely corrected by IR heterozygosity.
claims.source: Importantly, we found that the enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling otherwise associated with TCPTP-deficiency was significantly repressed, albeit not completely corrected by IR heterozygosity (Figure 6a–b).

results.result: POMC neurons from ad libitum fed mice exhibit heterogeneous responses to insulin: 50.9% (27/53) are inhibited (hyperpolarized), 37.7% (20/53) are unresponsive, and 11.3% (6/53) are activated (depolarized). Insulin-activated POMC neurons are located more medially and closer to the third ventricle.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C41-C45 provide converging electrophysiological evidence from whole-cell patch clamp recordings in Pomc-eGFP mice (Figure 1a-d). The data include quantitative measurements of membrane potential changes and firing rates for each neuronal subtype, with appropriate statistical analysis. The anatomical localization data (C45) is supported by camera lucida imaging.

results.result: TCPTP expression determines whether POMC neurons are activated or inhibited by insulin. Most insulin-inhibited (25/27) and unresponsive (11/20) POMC neurons express TCPTP, while most insulin-activated neurons (5/6) do not. TCPTP-deficiency or pharmacological inhibition increases the proportion of insulin-activated POMC neurons from 11% to 36% and 33%, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C46-C50 are supported by immunohistochemistry correlating TCPTP expression with electrophysiological responses (Figure 1e-f) and genetic/pharmacological manipulation experiments (Figure 1g-i). The data show consistent shifts in neuronal response proportions with TCPTP manipulation, though the mechanism linking TCPTP to electrophysiological responses remains unclear.

results.result: In diet-induced obesity, TCPTP protein levels in the mediobasal hypothalamus increase 6.3-fold, including in POMC neurons. This correlates with a shift in POMC neuronal responses: the proportion inhibited by insulin increases from 51% to 65%, while activated neurons decrease from 11% to 3%. TCPTP inhibition reverses this shift, increasing activated neurons to 37%.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C51-C54, C95-C97 are supported by immunoblotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-b), immunohistochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-d), and electrophysiological recordings (Figure 1k-l) in high-fat fed mice. The data demonstrate both increased TCPTP expression and altered neuronal responses in obesity, with pharmacological rescue experiments supporting causality.

results.result: Chronic (6 hr), but not acute (30 min), DREADD-mediated inhibition of POMC neurons increases hepatic glucose production, as evidenced by elevated pyruvate-induced glucose excursions. This is accompanied by decreased hepatic Il6 expression, reduced STAT3 phosphorylation, increased gluconeogenic gene expression (Pck1, G6pc), and decreased whole-body insulin sensitivity in hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 are supported by pyruvate tolerance tests (Figure 2c), hepatic gene expression and signaling data (Figure 2d-e, h), and hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps (Figure 2f-g). The temporal distinction between acute and chronic effects is well-documented. However, a caveat is that ~25% of AgRP neurons may express Pomc-Cre during development (C98), potentially confounding interpretation.

results.result: Chronic (6 hr), but not acute (30 min), DREADD-mediated activation of POMC neurons suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis, as shown by reduced pyruvate-induced glucose excursions. This is accompanied by elevated hepatic Il6 expression, increased STAT3 phosphorylation, and repression of gluconeogenic genes (Pck1, G6pc).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by pyruvate tolerance tests (Figure 2j) and hepatic molecular analyses (Figure 2k-l). The data mirror the inhibition experiments, providing complementary evidence. The same caveat regarding potential AgRP neuron involvement applies.

results.result: TCPTP deletion in POMC neurons enhances the insulin-mediated repression of hepatic gluconeogenesis in fasted mice. At insulin doses ineffective in controls, POMC-TC mice show improved pyruvate tolerance, increased hypothalamic Pomc and hepatic Il6 expression, enhanced hepatic STAT3 signaling, and greater repression of gluconeogenic genes (Pck1, G6pc).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by ICV insulin administration experiments with pyruvate tolerance tests (Figure 3b), qPCR (Figure 3c-d), and immunoblotting (Figure 3e). The data demonstrate enhanced central insulin sensitivity in POMC-TC mice. The elevated basal gluconeogenic gene expression in fasted POMC-TC mice (C67) is appropriately interpreted as compensatory.

results.result: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons improves whole-body glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity in chow-fed mice. This is characterized by lower fasted glucose and insulin levels, improved glucose and insulin tolerance, enhanced glucose infusion rates during clamps, and specifically enhanced insulin-mediated suppression of endogenous glucose production (not Rd). Hepatic insulin signaling (IR and AKT phosphorylation) is dramatically enhanced, while muscle and adipose tissue signaling is unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C77 are supported by comprehensive metabolic phenotyping including tolerance tests (Figure 4c-e), hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps (Figure 4f), hepatic gene expression (Figure 4g), and tissue-specific insulin signaling analyses (Figure 4h, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c-d). The data demonstrate liver-specific improvements in insulin sensitivity, consistent with a CNS-liver axis.

results.result: ICV insulin represses hepatic gluconeogenesis in fed but not food-restricted wild-type mice. In food-restricted POMC-TC mice, TCPTP deletion restores insulin responsiveness, enabling ICV insulin to suppress pyruvate-induced glucose excursions and dramatically reduce hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression while increasing Il6 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 are supported by feeding/fasting experiments with ICV insulin administration, pyruvate tolerance tests, and hepatic gene expression analyses (Figure 5b-c, e-h). The data demonstrate that TCPTP levels coordinate POMC neuronal responses with nutritional state. However, the mechanism linking feeding state to TCPTP regulation relies on prior work (C5, C6, C100, C101).

results.result: IR heterozygosity in POMC-TC mice partially corrects the enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling and reduces insulin-activated POMC neurons from 36% to 17%. This genetic rescue also normalizes hypothalamic Pomc expression, α-MSH staining in the PVH, and largely corrects the enhanced insulin-POMC-mediated repression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and improved glucose metabolism seen in POMC-TC mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 are supported by p-AKT immunohistochemistry (Figure 6a-b), electrophysiology (Figure 6c-d), gene expression and immunohistochemistry (Figure 6e-f), and metabolic phenotyping (Figure 6g-i, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a-d). The genetic rescue experiment provides strong evidence that TCPTP effects are mediated through IR signaling, though the correction is partial rather than complete.

results.result: In diet-induced obese mice, TCPTP deficiency in POMC neurons restores insulin responsiveness. While control obese mice are unresponsive to ICV insulin, POMC-TC obese mice show suppressed pyruvate-induced glucose excursions, increased hepatic Il6 expression and STAT3 signaling, repressed gluconeogenic gene expression, reduced fasted glucose and insulin levels, enhanced glucose infusion rates during clamps, and suppressed endogenous glucose production (with unchanged Rd).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 are supported by comprehensive metabolic analyses in high-fat fed mice including ICV insulin experiments (Figure 7a-d), metabolic measurements (Figure 7e-f), and hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps (Figure 7g-j). The data demonstrate that TCPTP deletion can overcome obesity-induced central insulin resistance, though the improvement is specific to hepatic glucose metabolism.

results.result: TCPTP-deficiency in POMC neurons increases c-Fos staining (a marker of neuronal activation) in the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH) of fasted mice, which is further enhanced by systemic insulin administration.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry (Figure 1m). The data provide in vivo evidence for enhanced POMC neuronal activation in TCPTP-deficient mice. However, c-Fos is an indirect marker of neuronal activity, and the similar hypoglycemia in both genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) suggests the effect is not due to differential glucose levels.

results.result: Background knowledge establishing the roles of insulin and leptin in hypothalamic regulation of metabolism, the anatomy and function of ARC POMC and AgRP neurons, the melanocortin circuit, and prior findings on IR signaling in these neurons. TCPTP is identified as an IR phosphatase whose abundance in the ARC is regulated by feeding and fasting.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C40 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims provide essential context for interpreting the novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work, though detailed verification of each citation is beyond the scope of this review.

results.result: Prior work from the authors establishes that TCPTP expression in hypothalamic neurons is increased by fasting (driven by corticosterone) and decreased by feeding (through proteasomal degradation). In AgRP neurons, TCPTP fluxes coordinate white fat browning and thermogenic activity with feeding, and also influence hepatic glucose metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C99-C103 are supported by citations to the authors' prior work (Dodd et al., 2017; Dodd et al., 2018; Loh et al., 2011). These findings provide critical context for the current study's hypothesis. The claims accurately represent the cited work, though they rely on the validity of those prior studies.

results.result: The Pomc-Cre transgene can delete in approximately 25% of NPY/AgRP neurons during early development, though the GFP reporter faithfully marks POMC neurons in adult mice and Cre-dependent AAV expression in adult Pomc-Cre mice occurs specifically in POMC neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C109, C110 are supported by appropriate citations (Padilla et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2018). These claims acknowledge an important limitation of the Pomc-Cre model while also providing evidence for specificity in adult mice. The authors appropriately note this caveat when interpreting their results, though it introduces some uncertainty about whether all observed effects are truly POMC-specific.

results.result: Potential mechanisms and translational relevance: In cardiomyocytes, insulin-induced PI3K signaling promotes mitochondrial fusion, and mitochondrial dynamics regulate neuronal function in AgRP and POMC neurons. In humans, obesity is associated with CNS insulin resistance, and intranasal insulin effects on hypothalamic function and glucose metabolism are impaired in overweight individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims provide mechanistic context and translational relevance. However, C104 explicitly notes that whether insulin affects mitochondrial dynamics in POMC neurons remains to be established, appropriately identifying a gap in knowledge.

results.result: POMC neuronal activation is accompanied by increased Pomc expression and processing to α-MSH, which is released from POMC neuronal terminals at the PVH to drive melanocortin-dependent responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by citations (Schneeberger et al., 2013; Varela and Horvath, 2012). These claims establish the link between POMC neuronal activity and downstream melanocortin signaling, which is central to interpreting the metabolic effects observed in the study.

results.result: POMC neurons activated or inhibited by insulin can repress or inhibit hepatic glucose production (HGP).
results.evaluation: Claim C3 states that both activated and inhibited POMC neurons can affect HGP, but the directionality is unclear from the claim itself. The DREADD experiments (C56-C64) show that chronic inhibition increases HGP while chronic activation decreases HGP, which is consistent but the claim as stated is ambiguous. The claim would be better stated as 'activated POMC neurons repress HGP while inhibited POMC neurons promote HGP.'
